title: Design-System Governance
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of design-system governance.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on design-system governance and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Design-System Governance is a professional technique for scaling styling decisions across components, repositories and product constraints.

content_blocks.title: Module 21 learning map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step module learning map: Advanced Arbitrary Values and CSS Composition → Styling in Large Monorepos → Advanced Browser Compatibility → Building a Professional Tailwind CSS Workflow. Lesson pages add code examples and practice.
content_blocks.caption: Learning map for Module 21, from the opening concept to a practical checkpoint.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Utility and token naming conventions; Rules for custom CSS; Shared component documentation; Design-token change management; Long-term maintainability. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to design-system governance, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating design-system governance. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to design-system governance.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to design-system governance.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A centered content section with a prominent heading and readable paragraph; rendering requires the configured Tailwind build.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying design-system governance without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Design-System Governance is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
